summary: In 5 AH, a coalition of Quraysh, Ghatafan, and other tribes — up to 10,000 fighters — laid siege to Madinah. On the strategic suggestion of Salman al-Farisi (RA), the Muslims dug a defensive trench (khandaq) that rendered the enemy cavalry ineffective, and the siege was ultimately broken by a combination of Muslim fortitude, strategic diplomacy, and divine intervention.
narrative:
The Battle of the Trench (Ghazwat al-Khandaq), also known as the Battle of the Confederate Forces (Ghazwat al-Ahzab), was the most existential threat the Muslim community faced in its first decade in Madinah. The coalition — called al-Ahzab (the Confederate Forces) — was assembled primarily by the Banu Nadir, a Jewish tribe previously expelled from Madinah, who visited the Quraysh, Ghatafan, and numerous other tribal confederacies to invite them against the Muslims. The Quraysh committed approximately 4,000 men under Abu Sufyan; Ghatafan provided 6,000; other tribes brought the total to approximately 10,000 — a force unprecedented in Arabian warfare at that time.

The Prophet ﷺ convened a council (shura) of companions to decide on the defensive strategy. Salman al-Farisi (RA) — a Persian companion who had encountered the technique in his homeland — proposed digging a trench along the exposed northern flank of Madinah (the other sides being naturally protected by terrain and date palm groves). The Prophet ﷺ accepted this proposal enthusiastically. Ibn Hisham records that the companions, including the Prophet ﷺ himself, worked on the trench in turns; the Prophet ﷺ worked with his own hands, carried earth, and recited poetry of encouragement alongside his companions. The work took approximately six days.

When the Confederate army arrived and found the trench, their cavalry — the decisive arm of Arabian warfare — was rendered ineffective. The siege lasted approximately twenty to twenty-seven days, during which the Muslim community endured considerable hardship: hunger was severe, the weather was bitterly cold, and there was constant fear of the massive enemy encampment. The Quran vividly recalls this moment: 'When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when eyes were blurred and hearts reached the throats, and you were thinking various thoughts about Allah. There the believers were tested and were shaken with a severe trembling.' (33:10-11)

A pivotal event during the siege was the treachery of the Banu Qurayza, a Jewish tribe within Madinah who had a treaty with the Muslims. Huyayy ibn Akhtab of the Banu Nadir persuaded Kaab ibn Asad, the chief of Banu Qurayza, to break the treaty and join the Confederate forces, potentially allowing an attack from the internal flank. This threatened to completely encircle the Muslims. The Prophet ﷺ dispatched Sad ibn Muadh and others to verify the situation; the Banu Qurayza confirmed their intention to break the treaty.

The siege was ultimately broken through two converging factors. Nuaym ibn Masud (RA), a Ghatafan tribesman who had secretly accepted Islam, offered to sow discord among the Confederate allies. He went to the Banu Qurayza, the Quraysh, and the Ghatafan in turn, suggesting to each that the others intended to abandon them — creating mutual suspicion that froze the coalition's ability to act. Then a fierce, bitterly cold wind of divine origin struck the camp: fires were extinguished, pots overturned, tents blown away. Abu Sufyan gave the order to withdraw. The Quran attributes the wind to Allah: 'O you who believe, remember Allah's favor upon you when armies came against you and We sent against them a wind and soldiers you could not see.' (33:9). The Prophet ﷺ returned to Madinah and declared: 'From now on we march against them; they will not march against us.'

Following the withdrawal of the Confederate forces, the Muslims turned to address the treaty violation by the Banu Qurayza. The Prophet ﷺ laid siege to their strongholds for approximately twenty-five days. The Banu Qurayza eventually surrendered and agreed to accept the arbitration of Sad ibn Muadh (RA), the chief of the Aws — the tribe with whom they had historically been aligned. Sad's ruling, delivered while critically wounded from the battle, was that the fighting-age men be executed, the women and children taken as prisoners of war, and the wealth distributed — consistent with the laws of war applied against a tribe that had actively committed treaty betrayal during a siege. The Prophet ﷺ accepted this arbitration and said: 'You have judged by the decree of Allah from above the seven heavens.' (Sunan Abi Dawud 3628 — authenticated). Classical scholarship, including Ibn Hisham, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, and Ibn al-Qayyim, presents this ruling as legally sound under the rules of war applicable to those who betray a treaty during active combat. The episode is the most frequently attacked incident of the Seerah by critics of Islam; the classical Sunni response is grounded in the specific conditions: prior treaty, active betrayal during siege, and formal arbitration by a party the Banu Qurayza themselves chose.
